utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Following the decision that was made on Friday in relation to the interview and the record of the interview of Mr. Lazarevic, the Chamber has been considering whether there are any implications that should be addressed. And we have concluded that there is one further step that ought to be taken. Rule 43(vi) seems to us to be in very simple, mandatory terms. "The tape," that's the record of the interview, "shall be transcribed if the suspect becomes an accused." Now, this case is -- doesn't fit exactly the time-scale of Rule 43, but plainly the provisions must apply to the situation of an accused who is interviewed following his indictment, just as it applies to the situation of an accused who was originally interviewed as a suspect. And when you look at the simple language there, it doesn't raise any issues of translation, it doesn't say anything about the language; it simply says the tape shall be transcribed, which means everything on the tape. And that means that the transcript in this case should have consisted of the whole of the tape-recording. Now, if the Prosecution intend to rely upon the transcript or at least the interview, intend to rely on the interview at all, then it has to be transcribed in its entirety. And even if the Prosecution do not -- decide that they do not intend to rely upon it, if the accused insists then it has to be transcribed in its entirety. Now, none of this affects the decision we've taken, that this was already exhibited, used in the trial, and is part of the evidence; however, we do now order the Prosecution to have the balance of the tape transcribed. I suspect Mr. Hannis is not in a position to say anything about how long that will take, and I do know that it could take some time; however, we take the view that everything else needs to be dropped to deal with this and it has to be done within a very tight time-scale. Should the provision of the transcript result in the need to review anything that's occurred so far in the trial, then we will review the situation and grant any necessary relief. For example, Mr. Bakrac might point to something in the transcript in B/C/S that somehow or other has alerted the accused to an issue that hasn't been adequately presented to the Tribunal, and we would have to consider whether some relief ought to be granted. But again, we will impose a pretty tight time-scale on that, to ensure that we introduce what's necessary under 43(vi) as quickly as possible to avoid it having any other implications for the trial. The specific order will be made tomorrow in the light of you having time to reflect on what we are saying and for Mr. Hannis, in particular, to consider the implications that this may have on the transcription facilities available. But we would expect to be told that this can be done pretty quickly in all the circumstances. There's also in this case, apart from any of the issues that arise about interpretation, the obvious discrepancy between the position of Mr. Lazarevic and four of the other accused whose interviews have been transcribed in full. And it's only right that there should not be seen to be any distinction among them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for this clarification, and I think I still owe you something. Pursuant to your order, I still have to request a corrected translation of -- I had to get a corrected translation of 5D194, paragraphs 2 and 3; this has been done and I believe it's been uploaded into e-court. Now, I can deal with that either in re-examination or we can do something now, but I complied with your order and I received information that this has already been done and it should be in e-court with Exhibit 5D194.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you aware of it, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not specifically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you should have time to consider whether there is any comment you wish to make. If, having done that, there's nothing you wish to say, then we can deal with this orally, but we'll postpone it until you've had an opportunity to consider the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, if I may, just one comment on what you raised. I had intended to bring up with you a related translation issue regarding the three upcoming witnesses. I know we discussed this yesterday, but I was advised again today that we still have a number of those that weren't translated. Mr. Bakrac explained to me that yesterday he was only talking about Lazarevic being completed. I propose perhaps -- I'll go back and see if perhaps the transcription of this interview can be done in-house. The other possibility is the interpreter who interpreted for that interview I understand now works at CLSS, so it might be easier if she were the one assigned to do it and I'll inquire to see if that's a possibility as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would invite you to avoid in any way inhibiting CLSS capacity to deal with other issues that arise at the moment for us. Your point about the translations -- translation of exhibits is noted, and that's going to have to be dealt with as and when it arises. Mr. Lazarevic, sorry about that, but it was necessary in your interests and in the wider interests of ensuring a fair trial for everyone here to address that issue. I'm sorry to have interrupted the cross-examination, but that can now continue. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. I think the last thing I had asked you about yesterday was a Supreme Command Staff --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- order about getting VJ commands and units out of schools. I'd like to show you now Exhibit P1462. I think this is what you made reference to. You said you hadn't seen the Supreme Command Staff order but you did see one from the 3rd Army. And is this the one that you were referring to dated the 13th of May from the 3rd Army command?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm familiar with this order because I complied with it with regard to the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I note that this says that: "Since NATO is firing at schools which VJ commands, units, and institutions are accommodated, I hereby order immediately relocate." So isn't it correct that at least some of those "civilian" targets that NATO was hitting at were things like schools in which VJ commands and units were located, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document from the army command that refers to the chief of the Supreme Command Staff, I understood it to refer to the whole of the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and I did not understand it to refer specifically and only to the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. But the corps command, as soon as this order was received, issued an order to its units to the effect that if there are any elements deployed in those civilian facilities, which they are, school buildings, to move out of those buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Next I want to show you Exhibit 5D372. General, this is a -- an order from you dated the 22nd of April, 1999, and it's entitled "moving the VJ -- VTJ, military territorial units, from inhabited places." Based -- do you have that on the screen? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Based on the date of that, can we infer that prior to the 22nd of April those units -- at least some of them had been located in inhabited places?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the examination-in-chief I explained that the military territorial units carry out tasks within larger inhabited areas in such a way that as -- within the framework of larger-scale tasks, they secure military facilities. So my answer is that parts of those units were performing their functions in larger towns, securing military facilities and other facilities that are important for the defence of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we see in item number 3 in your order, the second sentence says: "Do not allow civilian refugee groups to remain in the zones of defence of brigades." When you're talking about the zone of defence of a brigade, how big an area are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These areas vary in size, the surface areas differ, depending on the actual unit, but this refers to sectors of deployment of the units, "rejoni" so close to the sectors of deployment of the brigades, to provide assistance if there are any civilians so that they are not out in the open air, those refugees to assist the civilian authorities and the police, to find some accommodation for them that would be more appropriate. And these are areas 20 by 30 kilometres, sometimes 60 kilometres, 10, 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I know in your direct that we saw I think a couple of other orders of yours where you were trying to make provisions for the civilians and instructed subordinate units to in certain situations try to move them out of areas of anticipated combat with the terrorists or the KLA, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Terrorists and the security forces, because the KLA terrorists did not fight each other, that was the interpretation that I got. So let me just correct that. But the essence, the gist, of my orders was the following: Wherever possible, to assist this population, lest they should find themselves in cross-fire, under cross-fire, lest they should be used or abused, perhaps that would not be done on purpose, but they should not at any rate find themselves in the area where there are intensive conflicts between the security forces of the FRY and of the terrorist forces in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. And is it correct that in the first weeks of the war, the VJ was also engaged in constructing dummy positions, if you understand the term, to mislead NATO into bombing artificial assets, if you will?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as part of operational, tactical, and technical camouflage deception measures, all kinds of measures were used, dummy targets, decoys were set up, any number of those technical and tactical measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in one of those other orders of yours I saw an instruction that the civilians should not be placed in areas where the VJ was deployed; that's right too, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please look at this order in order to be able to see the context of this question? My colleague Mr. Hannis refers to some other order and draws some conclusions, yet we don't know what is actually in the order. I think it would be only fair if we were able to see, if Mr. Lazarevic were able to see this order that Mr. Hannis is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to look at it. If he doesn't remember, he can tell me he doesn't remember; if that's not correct, he can tell me. But I have limited time here and I don't want to look at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember, General, did you have some orders to that effect or not?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know very well that I issued orders, that combat positions in accordance with the combat plan of certain units at the battalion level should be relocated in order for the civilian population to be able to go back to their original places of residence. I know that, and I'm particularly referring to the Lab and Podujevo areas. Secondly, I don't recall the exact order in which I purportedly prohibited the placement of civilian population nearby, but I know that I did warn a number of times that security measures should be taken to prevent any risks, any endangering of the safety of the units in positions and in their sectors, that's true. And thirdly, in one of the orders right at the beginning of the war, I think the date is the 25th of March, I indicated or I referred to Article 70 of the Law on Defence, envisaging that commanders at the level of a regiment or a brigade may restrict the freedom of movement of the civilian population close to their sectors of deployment. But in my examination-in-chief I said that as far as I can remember no brigade commander had ever implemented this order; quite the contrary. They assisted wherever they could, they directed the civilian population to prevent any situation in which they could be targeted, either by NATO air-strikes or terrorists. So all my orders and warnings went in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Conflict with the terrorists and legitimate concerns that KLA or KLA sympathizers could be amongst any group of Kosovo Albanian civilians, I take it that you had concerns about those groups of civilians being located in or around the places where the VJ had command post or where their units were located in populated areas. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a general military issue, a question of doctrine, but to give you a specific answer, Mr. Prosecutor. The main command post where I spent most of my time as the commander is in the immediate vicinity of Albanian population, that's in the village of Badinovac [phoen] and the village of Kisnica, that was the fact throughout the war. And it never occurred to anyone to evacuate to other sectors away from the corps command. The army command was located there too. So I accept that as a matter of general principle that is so. There is a grave danger and many of the commanders asked for instructions. The medical battalion that was in the centre of Podujevo treating Albanian civilians reported to me several times that they said that they were afraid that they would be targeted by some attacks; fortunately, that never occurred but that would be the briefest possible answer I can give you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, if your instructions were to not permit the civilians to be in areas of VJ deployment and that they should be moved out of areas where combat with the KLA was about to or might be about to take place, if they were not to be in the -- I forget what the term was I used at the beginning - the zones of defence of the brigades, I suggest to you in Kosovo at that time, that doesn't leave many places for those civilians to be, does it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this question is quite long, so I would like to ask the Trial Chamber's permission to -- I would like to say that I did not say in my response that civilians could not be in the zones of the units; quite the contrary. I ordered that special elements be set up to protect these people if they ever found themselves close to the sectors. So that is the gist of my answer. And now as to how many civilians there actually were in Kosovo and Metohija, I can only say that as far as I know some larger towns had even more inhabitants than before the war, Gnjilane, Podujevo, Prizren, and those were the reports that I had been receiving. There were many people in Pristina, too, so that was the knowledge that I had at the time. Now, as for the actual number, I really don't know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were aware, though, that huge numbers of civilians had left Kosovo in the first two weeks of the war, right? You couldn't help but know that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the fact that many people had left Kosovo and Metohija because it was a battle-field, and this caused serious consequences for everyone concerned. People were leaving in all directions, in the -- and in one of my reports I reported to the army commander, so he was aware of that, and he reported further up. So this is not something that we were not aware of. This caused us some concern. As far as I can remember, I said that this was a humanitarian concern and it was also a concern from the standpoint of military doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we have a quick look at Exhibit P2930. I don't know if this is the document you referred to, but it's a Pristina Corps regular combat report dated the 31st of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we can scroll down, I'm not sure where the reference is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You may have seen this shown to another witness, General, but it talked about MUP and military territorial units channelling Siptar refugees to the Albanian border.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we may have to go to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first have to answer that I did not refer to this report. This is not a combat report from the Pristina Corps command, but from a command group that was in Djakovica at the time because the forward command post had not yet been set up. So this is not in Djakovica, it's in a village of Mazre. As far as I was able to see, that's a couple of kilometres away from the Albanian border. And I saw this here, this document was shown on one or two occasions to witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My misstatement, General. But do you recall having seen such a report? You said you sent it to the -- you sent a report about that to the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not based on this report. It was based on the report of the brigade commanders in whose areas the border crossings were. At the time this report could not have reached the corps command; it couldn't have reached the corps command in the following ten days, because in the night between the 27th and the 28th Djakovica and the communications centre were destroyed in the NATO air-strikes. The forward command post, or rather, command group was established on the 9th of April, and it could not send reports to the corps command in written form.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me go then to one of the reports from a brigade commanders, this would be P2046. General, this is a regular combat report from Colonel Dikovic of the 37th Motorised Brigade dated the 28th of March, 1999. And the last item under 9.3 before his name he says: "In the forthcoming operations in the Vocnjak village sector, we expect to encounter shelters with several thousand civilian refugees. We request instructions." Do you recall having received this report or having been advised of the contents of this report about those civilian refugees?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm at this point in time whether this is how it was reported, but I do know about these events. I know that he requested the treatment of civilians in the area of combat activities; and if I may be allowed to say this, as far as I can see, this report was not signed by Nikovic, one of his commanders signed it. And the way I understand this officer here is the following: This was a combat group, it wasn't yet a brigade in the beginning of the war. And in his assessment, because in item 4 at the beginning it says that terrorist forces are firing on army units from that village, so he expected there to be conflicts and he feared that this would lead to refugees fleeing. And he said that he did not have the strength to protect the civilian population from those hostilities. He couldn't help them or get them out of the area of combat activities, and if I may add, this is a unit or part of a unit with no combat experience as yet. And yesterday we saw how on the 7th of August the commander of the 15th Brigade informed the corps command in 1998 when activities against terrorist forces were interrupted if civilians were observed or humanitarian organizations or diplomats in the immediately vicinity. Through the centre -- through the intelligence centre he received a reply that firing should be stopped and fighting should be interrupted in order to avoid imperilling the life of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You heard evidence in this trial from some of the survivors of what we've called the massacre at Izbica, and so you're aware that there are allegations that that took place on the 28th of March, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have heard testimony here that between the 25th and the 28th or 29th of March, there were testimonies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know that Vocnjak village is approximately 2 kilometres or less south of Izbica?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that off the top of my head. It's possible. One can see that precisely on a map. It's the area of Gornja Drenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, if we can take a moment to look at P615 at page 17. And I'll be looking to enlarge on the right one-third of the page and halfway down in that right-hand column. Okay. That's good. General, do you -- can you see Izbica on that map?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you'll see below that, almost directly south, Vojnik, yeah?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says Vojnik here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's the nearest village to Izbica shown on that map, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this map it is. I want to say to the best of my recollection there's no place called Vojnik, it's Vocnjak. I have never heard of a village in Kosovo and Metohija called Vojnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is there a document reflecting the reply from the Pristina Corps to this request for instructions on what to do about those civilians? We haven't seen that yet, have we?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I might say that we have seen at least five or six documents, which at the very beginning of the war defined with precision the way the civilian population is to be treated, at least five or six documents or orders as to how to treat civilians, how to take care of them, how to assist them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, General. I understand that we've seen some of those general instructions, but I'm asking have we seen a document that shows the specific reply to this specific request from Colonel Dikovic about what to do about the expected several thousand civilians that he thought they were going to come across in the Vojnik village area. Have we seen such a document?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we have not seen a response to this combat report. I can assess how this question was answered, and we will have an opportunity probably --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm going to have to try and cut you off more often today I think because I'm trying to get done as soon as possible. Thank you, General. The next one I want to show you is a P2024. This is another regular combat report from a different subordinate brigade, the 125th Motorised Brigade, and this one is dated 27 April 1999. It appears to be a telegram.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in English we have to go to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's on the first page for you, General, it's about ten lines up from the bottom, and the English says: "During the day at 0800 hours, a column of Siptar civilians was formed on the following axis," and further on: "We believe they want to pull out from the sector of operations of our forces in the general area of the Ramoc facility." And this relates, does it not, to the action, the so-called Reka action, that was going on in that area west and north-west of Djakovica at that time?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in specific terms as regards this date and this movement of civilians at the time of those activities, K-73 testified about that. That was in a part of the 125th Brigade, I assume it refers to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's right, General. Thank you. Now, I want to go one more time to what you probably perceive as one of my favourite topics, the Joint Command. Exhibit P2166 is the document we've talked about before with other witnesses in this case. If we could have that up on the screen. And, General, I can give you a hard copy because this one's several pages. This is the minutes of the meeting of the operations inter-departmental staff for the suppression of terrorism in Kosovo on the 29th of October, 1998. Do you recall having seen this one and having heard it discussed here with a number of witnesses?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that several witnesses spoke about this and answered questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the reason -- well, one of the reasons I show it to you is that I guess I have a question for you. Do you have reason to doubt the authenticity of this document? Do you have any personal knowledge that leads you to believe it's not authentic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how I can confirm or deny this. I see that there's a stamp there, that it comes from the archives, according to the protocol and the format of this document, it seems to be regular. I did not hear until my arrival in the Detention Unit of anybody referred to as an operations inter-departmental staff at the high state level. I did not have any knowledge of the existence of such a body, but from the technical standpoint, I'm not an expert, but it appears to me to be -- to be a record, minutes which have their registration number, date, signature, that's a technical issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you've seen the list of the people attending that meeting. You personally know or are acquainted with most of those people, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you've seen the minutes and you've seen that every -- almost everyone attending this meeting or at least everyone who speaks makes reference to the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. And General Pavkovic, your immediate superior, is the one who made the presentation speaking on behalf of the Joint Command, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. The Prosecutor is drawing my attention to the last passage on page 1 in the Serbian language. I don't understand these to be General Pavkovic's words, but rather, the words of the person taking the minutes where he says "I'll speak on behalf of the Joint Command," if that's what you're asking me about. The way I understand it, the person who was taking the minutes was the one who spoke in those terms about General Pavkovic. These are all statements, if they were statements or contributions to the discussion, but they are not in quotation marks. So these are not direct quotations, it's just somebody's notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is -- are they not supposed to be the words of Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understood the question to concern General Pavkovic, saying that he was speaking on behalf of the Joint Command, and that's what I focused on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The English to which your attention is -- the English of the passage to which your attention's being drawn is a summary of what Milosevic said introducing the session, and the last thing he said was General Pavkovic would then present the proposals of the Joint Command; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I see it now, it's in the paragraph before the one I was looking at. I wasn't sure what paragraph I should focus on, I didn't get precise instructions, but I says General Pavkovic will present the proposals of the Joint Command, but I cannot confirm that these are the words of the president of the FRY, maybe they are but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hannis will now ask you the question he's working up to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, we see at the last page that these minutes were compiled by Lieutenant-General Slavoljub Susic, did you know him? It's on the very last page.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the war as far as I can recall, I saw him on one occasion but I didn't know who he was or what post he held. After the war, however, I think I did have an opportunity and I know who the person is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the list of attendees on the first page his name is the last one mentioned and it says Lieutenant-General Dr. Susic. Do you know what kind of doctor he was? He appears to have some special title.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, really. Probably something to do with military science. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, don't you expect that in a meeting of this nature, involving President Milosevic, President Milutinovic, the president of the Federal Assembly, the top generals in the army and top police officials, don't you expect that the person chosen to take the notes would be somebody who could do a fairly good job of taking notes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I believe this really calls for speculation. We know that Mr. Susic is heading the military cabinet of FRY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There may be the answer, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'd like this witness to agree with me that you wouldn't have a slob take the minutes of this kind of a meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the answer is the person taking the minutes would normally be expected to be the one doing so because of the position he held. If the witness doesn't know, he doesn't know whether he's a slob when it comes to taking minutes or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, I would ask you to look at these minutes and wouldn't you agree with me that they appear to be quite detailed and rather precise?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to object to that, Your Honour -- he's asking the General to indicate that they're precise, how can he without speculation know that they are precise or not. The document is what it is. That's all he can establish if he hasn't been there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that these minutes are quite detailed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, no, please deal with the objection. The objection was that they were quite detailed and precise, so it extended to both.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I change my question for now to just detailed. But I would suggest that we've heard evidence from this witness and others talking about the Joint Command notes and the problems with those; by contrast, I think this witness could give us some sort of opinion about whether these notes were as good or better than what we've seen in the Joint Command meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you would rephrase the question to be appear to be quite detailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, General, that these minutes appear to be quite detailed?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm leafing through it now, trying to recognise something precise. As far as my knowledge of the situation on the ground goes, there's a lot of information here which I cannot recognise from the viewpoint of numbers, large numbers, maybe this was actually said at the meeting concerning the terrorist forces and the numbers of casualties and those taken prisoner. Well, there's a lot of things written down here, whether it's precisely noted down or not -- well, it's 16 pages long. A lot of effort has been put into it. But what concerns me is that I do not know of the existence of such a body, an operations staff. I don't know about something like that. I didn't hear about it at the time. Here I see that this staff issued orders and decisions, that it was chaired by the president of the state, that there were officials there from the army and the police. I knew that the corps commander with the army commander and the Chief of the General Staff sometimes went to see the president, but it's only here that I've seen such documents and come across minutes like these. So these are minutes, it was not a stenographic record, as I can see from what it says here. And I can neither confirm nor deny that this is correct, what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, on the first page we have the note that opening the session President Milosevic informed the members of this group that General Pavkovic was going to present the proposals of the Joint Command. So there's our first reference to the Joint Command, and following that, still on the first page, it says: "Speaking on behalf of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, General Pavkovic reminded," there's a second reference to Joint Command. And then we see General Pavkovic talking about the plan to suppress terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija, and you were aware that there was such a plan, you told us about that there was a five-phase plan. This is page 3 in your B/C/S copy, I believe, right? There was such a plan to suppress terrorism?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And he lists some seven tasks in connection with that plan. Number 2 was organizing, equipping, and coordinating the operations of the MUP and VJ to oppose terrorist forces. That's something that you know was done, correct? Prior to October 29th of 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And number 7, that's on page 4, it talks about disarming all Siptar villages which are known to be armed. You know that's something that was being done between July and September of 1998 because you were involved in that, were you not?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't accept that this corresponds to what I was saying and what I participated in. I spoke about the border belt where the army was in charge, where not even a hunting rifle could be brought in without approval, without a licence, let alone establishing terrorist bases. As for the rest, I didn't speak about that because it was not within the competency of the army. And if I may be allowed to comment on this further, on my understanding of this, my knowledge from that period is that members of the Albanian national community voluntarily returned without any consequences, no legal or judicial consequences, they returned the weapons to the forces of public law and order, primarily the forces of the MUP, in large quantities. And these illegal weapons, these illegitimate weapons were collected. That's what was done. And what I see here --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you trying to use up my time? You were involved in disarming Siptar villages, right? Maybe you were only in the border belt, but you were involved in that in 1998. That is something that was done pursuant to the plan to suppress terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What is not correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. It's not correct that I participated in disarming armed Albanian villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were involved in it because you were at the forward command post of the Pristina Corps command, you attended meetings of the Joint Command where you talked about those operations going on. So I say you were involved in it to that extent, were you not?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the exchange of information between the military and the police in quite a different way regarding where measures should be taken to take away illegally -- illegal weapons, especially in the border belt. And I understand the meeting of the Joint Command in a different way than was put by the Prosecutor. Thirdly, as far as I understood the interpretation, there was a mention of operations conducted to disarm armed settlements.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the Joint Command meetings you attended, did you not talk about villages in which the surrender of arms was going to be undertaken that day or the following day?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I talked about the necessity of the police, together with the military, to enter the border belt villages, to negotiate, to talk to the people there so that they would return illegal weapons, since such weapons were not supposed to be there inside the border belt. Well, one shouldn't have them anywhere, let alone the border belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Could you go to the bottom of page 5. This is still General Pavkovic talking about what was done under the plan. At the bottom my English translation says: "Eighth, large quantities, over 150 tonnes of weapons and ammunition were confiscated and handed over in the course of implementing the plan" - I'm on page 5 of the English - and next I think you have to turn the page, General, to page 6. It says: "93 Siptar villages were disarmed, 31 in Djakovica municipality." Is that consistent with your knowledge and information about what was done in connection with the plan in July through September of 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, based on the combat documentation that I could see back in 1998, when preparing for defence states that the villages in a large number of municipalities voluntarily - and I reiterate voluntarily - returned whatever weapons they had to the MUP organs. There were announcements via local radio stations calling for them to surrender their weapons without any consequences. That is the knowledge I have pertaining to that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you have a quarrel with the translations? My English says: "93 Siptar villages were disarmed." It doesn't say anything about whether that occurred voluntarily or forcibly. I take that to mean that their weapons were turned in.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about what I knew based on the documentation I could see based on the reports, which stated that villages voluntarily handed over their weapons first and foremost to MUP organs --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I'm not saying it wasn't voluntary and this document doesn't say it wasn't voluntary.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are correct. I do not dispute that. However, I'm telling you what I know about it, that's how I understood your question. The same is in the Serbian, disarmed, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in Serbian does "disarmed" have a connotation that it was done other than voluntarily? I don't understand why you're arguing with me about this.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess we're arguing about the word "disarmed." Perhaps in your view this includes coercion, force, that it had to be done, that was the meaning of "disarmed." However, "handed over" or "returned" --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, excuse me. Just a simple objection. Mr. Hannis should simply repeat his question. He didn't ask General Lazarevic what the document says, but rather what he knows about it. If you look at the question -- well, that's what we heard. I don't know what your intention was. That's the thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's Mr. Lazarevic who has insisted on answering the question by reference to the document. The question that was put was to quote what's in the -- this document and then say: Is that consistent with your knowledge and information about what was done in connection with the plan in July through September? Now, what's wrong with that question? And is Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing's wrong with the question, but he was replying to the question. Mr. Lazarevic had never seen this document before. He cannot know what is contained in something he never saw, and he wasn't present at the meeting. That's what I wanted to say a minute ago. We had three witnesses who were present at the meeting and were not asked any questions about it. He's talking about what he knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, he's not being asked about what happened at the meeting. He's asked about whether -- what did happen at the meeting is consistent with his own personal knowledge, and he has insisted on explaining that by reference to documents. Now, whether Mr. Hannis wants to then explore that further is a matter for him, but there's nothing wrong with the question that's been put. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. Maybe there is a misunderstanding. When you say "referred to the document," but he didn't refer to this document but rather to combat documentation from 1998 in general. He didn't mean this specific document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I know that --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but the combat documentation from that period. It was my understanding that we were discussing this document alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila's objection is he shouldn't be answering it by reference to other documents; he should be answering it by reference to his own knowledge, and indeed that's what the question tries to obtain. Mr. Hannis, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, a little farther down on page 6 there's a reference: "9th item, 287 of our soldiers were put out of action, 62 from the VJ, and 225 from MUP. 79 of our soldiers, 22 from the VJ, and 57 from MUP were killed while the plan was being implemented." Is that consistent with what you knew about the extent of losses to the VJ during July to September 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with the information for 1998 in general, but as to this specific number I can't tell you anything. I know there were 45 soldiers killed and 196 wounded in that year; however, as far as this period goes, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you actually saying that you're not familiar with the figures for damage sustained to personnel through the anti-terrorist operations in the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Personally, back in 1998, I did not conduct any analysis of the implementation of tasks. Towards the end of that year, I know that we made an analysis, but it was an analysis for the whole of 1998. I didn't analyse any casualties for this specific period of two or two and a half months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm talking now of general experience, and it's related to the last 20 years or so. But my impression is that the public are very well-informed of casualties in warfare throughout the world where they have an interest, and it therefore comes as a bit of a surprise to me that the man in charge at the border doesn't know how many casualties there were during a particular operation. So can I take it that senior officers in the army at that time would not be absolutely up-to-date on the deaths and serious injuries being sustained by their men during particular operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Honour, it is a very sensitive matter, at least in the interpretation I received, hopefully wrongly, I heard -- well, there were casualties at the border, I saw people being killed, but I thought -- I wasn't asked about that. Here we are talking about two and a half months and the number of soldiers killed in the area of Kosovo and Metohija. I cannot confirm whether this figure was precise or not. I had my own data concerning the border. I know who was killed when throughout the year, but I did not deal with this analysis, I did not attend any meetings pertaining to this period analysing the situation. And as I said, or rather, I quoted a very precise figure to you which pertains to the whole year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you able to give us the figure for the border belt for the period that the report relates to, July to September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could tell you that precisely, but after the break I would have to go through my notes. I don't want to confuse either you or myself. I have data by months and by intensity, the number of wounded and killed and missing for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General, I would like to ask you to go back a page for a minute then, page 5. And General Pavkovic is talking about the losses suffered by the terrorists during these operations. Do you find that under the seventh item?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He mentions the number of 32.594, and he breaks that down by saying 3500 were killed. And farther down he says 560 were liquidated in special operations conducted by State Security Service. Can you tell us what the difference is between killed and liquidated in this context?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that at the beginning of item 7 there is a mention made of available information and evaluations --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- which leads me to conclude that these figures are evaluations. I'm trying to be precise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, you're not being asked to comment on the figures yet. You're being asked what the difference is between being killed and being liquidated. Mr. Hannis is limited for time, you must concentrate on the individual questions that he's asking you and answer these questions, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand this, Your Honour. I don't understand these two bullets, what they mean. I don't understand what liquidated and special operations conducted by the State Security Service means.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the answer may be, Mr. Hannis, it's the same word in Serbian in both passages, and there is no difference. And I apologise if there's been a confusion in your mind, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I just noticed that there is a misinterpretation on this page under 7, the last word. In Serbian it's "terrorist" -- the first paragraph of -- when it says seventh, it's underlined and the last word is in English is "September" and in Serbian is "terrorist." So I would suggest just for the clarity of this document that Mr. Hannis returns this to the CLSS for a proper translation because it's obviously not corresponding one to the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, does the Serbian say 32.594 terrorists up to 30th September?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, it says up to 3609 terrorists, I don't know what that means, that is a fact, but that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So September is not referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, it doesn't say 30th September at all. It says 36.09 terrorists --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that -- I see --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And from the English text you might get the wrong conclusion, which is not contained in the Serbian original. That's only thing what I wanted to draw the attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It seems unclear -- it seems unclear, Mr. Hannis, what that passage actually says.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with regard to one point, it's been my experience that in translating dates if it's 36.09 and I think there's a question mark whether the 36 should be 30, but 09 is typically translated with the name of the month in English. That's what we see on documents that are 06091998, will be translated 06 September 1998. I think that's a standard practice in CLSS. But I don't know of the existence of the last word being terrorist.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a suggestion to make. Perhaps Mr. Lazarevic can read it out loud and it will be as clear as day; very simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Possibly. Mr. Lazarevic, would you read from the word "seventh" to the end of that sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Seventh, based on available information and evaluations carried out during the implementation of the plan, losses, for various reasons, by the terrorists or on the terrorist side are 32.594 to 36.09," I think there is another dot there, "terrorists."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we should use some common sense, and it's clear that the fifth digit is missing. It's very simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you say that it should be 36.090 or something like that, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it says that the losses were 32.000 to something of terrorists, then it has to be a figure. It says based on evaluations carried out. This is an evaluation, an assessment, and the assessment is 32.594 to 36.000-something. It's between or from/to. That's why the difference there. It's not a date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, it may be that having the translation revised does not necessarily answer all outstanding questions, but nevertheless that should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Aleksic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, another objection concerning this portion. To us attorneys at law in Serbia, they say that we're extremely poor in math, but by adding these figures up you do not arrive anywhere near the figures mentioned and to me it is highly illogical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That may be because whoever was at the meeting is even worse at math than the Serbian attorneys, but we can hear more of that in due course. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I do have a disagreement about the math. I think if you add all the numbers you will come close to it. And what Mr. Fila said it may be a range, that may be correct as well because you will see the second item is 5 to 6.000 terrorists, another one is 8500 to 9500, another entry is 6000 to 6500 so if you add the low end and the high end you may come up with a number very close to what Mr. Fila suggested But be that as it may we will get that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That means that the missing number is 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 36409 is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, 36094, which would be 3 and a half thousand -- is it 3 and a half thousand of a difference? And that may be a thousand out as well because there are 2.500 -- oh, no, 3.500 in the range. So it's 3.500 of a difference it's 36.094.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Back to the law, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, below the 560 were liquidated it says: "In addition to the above-mentioned losses a total of 1.344 were put out of action in operations on the state border ..." So this is an area that you can perhaps help us with. It says: "666 liquidated," I don't know if that's the same word for killed. Is that consistent with what you knew about the number of terrorists killed during the implementation of this plan -- this says between 25 July and 25 September 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can be rather more precise concerning this item when talking about the border. My knowledge, should I be given permission to state what I find in my notes, mention a figure for the entire year at the border there were between 4 and 500 casualties on the terrorist side, again I repeat that this was an assessment, and captured or taken prisoner or detained, since it was not a state of war --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the number of those detained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- However, I refer to the entire 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the number for those detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My knowledge for the entire year at the border is around 600 -- 400 to 600. I cannot be precise, but I can locate that in my notes, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, a part of the answer, 33, 14, was not recorded in the transcript. I believe the witness said that as for the wounded ones, it was always an assessment because we couldn't find out precisely how many. But he says, I can find -- I can find that in -- the assessment I can find in my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General Pavkovic -- General Lazarevic, are your numbers only for the state border with Albania? Does it include the state border with Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Macedonia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from where were you receiving that information? Who provided that information to you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade commander who was in charge of securing the border in-depth and securing the border belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So one possible explanation for the differences between the numbers you told us and the numbers that are listed or noted down in this minutes as being reported by General Pavkovic is that General Pavkovic reported higher numbers, exaggerated numbers? That's one possibility, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether these are his words, whether the figures from the table are his, whether he exaggerated anything. By your permission, Your Honours, I also saw a document from the 3rd Army command. We saw who the author was, and he paints the picture in completely -- in a completely different way. The figures there are 10- to 15-fold less than these. I don't know whether the army command was wrong or maybe General Pavkovic put forth other figures at this meeting I'm now put in a position to explain something which I can't. Had I been in that meeting, I would have remembered a thing or to and I could assist you. But as far as I know, and this was a Prosecution exhibit dated the 2nd of October, it was a report from the 3rd Army Command referring to this very issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, is it a convenient time to interrupt you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall rise now and resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge, I would tell you I have received that translation of 5D194 and I have no objections to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall allow the new translation to be substituted for the previous.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you were just saying that some of those numbers attributed to General Pavkovic were not consistent with the numbers as you knew them to be. I would direct you to page 12 of the B/C/S, it's the very top of page 12 in the English, and for you it's probably is little more than halfway down. And in English it says: "In General Perisic's view" -- I'm sorry, I'll wait for you. It's three paragraphs up from the reference to President Milutinovic. Do you find that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. President Milutinovic, and then just in front of what -- before what he says.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And it says: "In General Perisic's view, 'the situation in Kosovo and Metohija does not correspond to the way it is depicted by certain members of the Joint Command.'" Two things about that, it appears we have a statement put in quotation marks, which suggests those are the actual words of General Perisic, and he's referring to the Joint Command, right? That's what quotation marks would mean in a document like this.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that you put quotation marks when words are being quoted. I don't know whether the italics in the original mean that. In Serbian orthography there are quotation marks and they are used when you are quoting somebody. Here what is being put by Mr. Prosecutor -- I see two other marks in the sentence below this one that may indicate that this is a quotation, but I cannot be sure if that is indeed so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The other question I have about that is that I suggest to you this may be a reference to what General Pavkovic has said earlier in the meeting regarding his summary of the plan for combatting terrorism as carried out between July and September 1998. Don't you think that's what he's referring to or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, is that something Mr. Lazarevic is in any better position to deduce than we are, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, only to the extent that he has a personal belief that the numbers are incorrect, based on his own personal knowledge, where you and I might not share that same knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the point you're putting is does he think this is a reference to the inaccurate presentation of the figures?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, could you please deal with that, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My knowledge based on the documents that I had an opportunity to review contemporaneously at the relevant time and in my preparations for the defence, and now I'm referring specifically to the documents related to this two-and-a-half month period from the 3rd Army is completely different from the information that is presented here in terms of the casualty figures of -- for the terrorist forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that document of the 3rd Army was prepared by whom?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood Lieutenant-General Tomislav Mladenovic, who testified in General Pavkovic's defence, to say that he personally had drafted this analysis as the operations officer of the 3rd Army. I understood that to be the effect of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I have no problems with Mr. Hannis's questions, but I have a problem with the interpretation. As long as we have this on our screens, you see here your initial -- the initial word in the English translation has the quotation marks "in General Perisic's view," and then we have the quotation mark. If you look at the Serbian language - and the Judge sitting next to you knows that language - there is nothing of the sort, there are no quotation marks. And then there is another passage where you have some other kind of markings, that's the fourth paragraph in Serbian, yes, it says: "We have to do everything," and so on, and there are some marks in Serbian, and in your translation there are again quotation marks. And that is why Mr. Hannis puts it to the witness that this is a quote, because there are quotation marks in English but not in Serbian. I don't apologise, Mr. Hannis, for interrupting you, but I'm doing that because now we have this document on our screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will see, Mr. Fila, if I'm reading the right paragraphs that there is different script used for the parts which are in quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's -- that is so in one location, but that does not mean that there are quotation marks there. This is something that somebody inferred. You could just put those words in italics in the English version, and if you look two passages down there is no italics. We just see some markings there, they look like arrow points, and then it just goes on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, are both passages that you have taken issue with not in italics?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are, yes, but this is just an inference on the part of somebody that the italics mean that this is a quote. In Serbian, that's not -- that's not so; that may be so in English, but it's not so in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is a matter also in which you can make submissions in due course. Please proceed on the basis you're proceeding, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I'll try to speed this up. In addition to General Pavkovic and Mr. Milosevic being attributed to having used the term "Joint Command" and what we just saw regarding General Perisic, I will tell you that at page 7 of the English and the B/C/S we have General Lukic attributed to as using the term "Joint Command." We also see it for Mr. Minic on page 10 of the B/C/S, page 9 of the English. We see it in connection with Mr. Milutinovic on page 12 of the English and the B/C/S; and Mr. Sainovic on page 13, in both the English and the B/C/S. Do you think General Susic made a mistake ten times by writing down "Joint Command"?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I did not speak about any mistakes by General Susic in what he wrote down on the basis of what the Prosecutor just listed, I can see that if it is indeed the way it is written here, that more people were using this term. And I as an officer at that time understood this term in a particular, very specific way, and on page 16, if you read those conclusions, I'm quite sure that I was correct in my understanding of the Joint Command at that time because if this is what the president of the state says, so he's not adopting the conclusions of the Joint Command but those of the MUP staff leader and of the Pristina Corps commander. And to this day, this is the way that I have understood it as I sit here, that when the army and the police carry out some specific actions down there, that somebody use that term, and this term appears to have been used, as is indicated here, both by the Chief of the General Staff, the president of the state, and other people too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know if you mentioned that the presentation by Mr. Minic, president of the Chamber of the Federal Assembly, that was also adopted, correct? That's what it says at the same place you saw the references to the reports by Lukic and Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have no reason to disbelieve that this is what is said next to Mr. Minic's name, but let me repeat once again. I understand that whenever they refer to it, when they use this term, that they're talking about the combined operations and combined engagement of the army and the police in Kosovo and Metohija in the effort to fight terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Which they all agree is called the Joint Command, right, Mr. Milosevic included?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is, I think, crossing the line and asking -- we've been doing this exercise for some time now and I've tried to resist jumping up, but I do not believe that the Prosecution can ask this witness to speculate and conclude what several individuals concluded or had the same idea, et cetera, that is sheer speculation and is improper questioning and I think we're approaching a point where the Prosecution has exhausted his real questions and is going into this fantasy world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- More speculation than my question was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your question, though, has by this witness been answered a number of times. He's stated what his understanding is, and this assertion is in the context pure argumentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will move on then to P2016.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, this is a combat report from you to the 3rd Army command and the Supreme Command Staff dated 25 April 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we need to go to item 2.1 which is on the first page of the B/C/S, but we need to go to the top of page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This regards activities, effects, consequences and others and it says: "Operations of combing the terrain and breaking up STS continue in line with the decision of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija." This is in your combat report to the 3rd Army and the Supreme Command on 25 April 1999. So if this is a nonexistent body, why are you referring to actions in line with the decision of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of more than 120 combat reports generated during the war, I'm sure that this is one or perhaps even one and only report in which a mention is made of the term "Joint Command." For a very simple reason that as far as these actions are concerned that were carried out together with the police, orders had been prepared bearing the letterhead and the title of the Joint Command. The duty officer in the operations centre of the corps that day has in front of him on his desk that order, because he's following the situation, and he made this reference, saying this is being done in accordance with this order for Rugovska Klisura, Rugova gorge, and whatever action was being carried out at the time. And we saw the Prosecution exhibit indicating that there were 15 or 16 such documents, and this is the simple explanation. And by your leave, Your Honours, let me say that I am reporting to the Supreme Command Staff and the army command, probably in the last part of this report it is indicated that everything is carried out in accordance with the -- with my decision, the decision of the corps commander. I can't see it now, but I know that this is the format of all those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we look next at Exhibit P2042.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, this is a daily operational report to the Pristina Corps command and also to the 2nd Army for information. It comes from Colonel Dikovic of the 37th Motorised Brigade on the 23rd of March. And if you'll go to item 15, conclusion, it's on page 2 of the English. "Pursuant to the decision of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, strictly confidential number 455-54 of 22 March 1999," and that's one we looked at yesterday, he describes what the 37th has done. That Exhibit was P2031, 455-54. So the order he got must have contained a reference to the Joint Command as well as your 455 number in order for him to be reporting back and making reference to both of those, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We saw this document yesterday, 455-4 [as interpreted] and with this title, and that's why the reference is made. He's reporting to me as the commander, not the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we look next at P2017.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, this is a combat report from the 3rd Army command to the General Staff dated the 29th of April, 1999, and it's under item 2.1, so we need to go to page 2 of the English. And for you it's on page 1, three lines up from the bottom. It says -- or actually four lines it should start I guess. "Measures were under" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, but I don't want line 21 -- but what is missing there is 455-54, not just 4, but that's important because then we can know what the reference is, to what document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It says: "Measures were undertaken to block the above sectors and carry out tasks in line with the Joint Kosovo and Metohija Command decision." And this is from the 3rd Army command to the Supreme Command Staff, so General Pavkovic is also aware of the existence of the Joint Command and making reference to it in a combat report; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am bold enough to say that this is not so. I'm saying that because I don't want to offend anyone, but that really is not so. And if I am allowed to read the context of item 2.1, the first sentence is the army commander is reporting to the Supreme Command Staff that the corps units are carrying out tasks related to my decision. So I am in command of those units. And then whoever is drafting this report is saying that in Malo Kosovo, since there is an order that is entitled an order from the Joint Command, it is in existence, and the -- it is said that a task will be carried out in accordance with this order that bears the title of the Joint Command, but this is very important. The first sentence just -- the first sentence after item 2.1 is very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you finished?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, one possible explanation for what you just said is that General Pavkovic was a member of the Joint Command. This wording then would be consistent with that state of facts, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know - and I'm sure this is so - we showed practically all the documents that have this letterhead of the Joint Command, we saw those documents, we saw what they are, what log numbers they bear, and I'm absolutely sure that this is the -- what the reference is to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then he would otherwise have said that this is carried out in accordance with his order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, can you not answer my question yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The reason I pushed you a bit about the Joint Command is because of what you went through in 2001 suggests to me that of all the people we've seen so far you seem to be the most aware of the possible problems created by somebody like the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we look at Exhibit 5D475, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move to that, Mr. Hannis, just one piece of clarification arising from this. You've explained to us a number of times that "Joint Command" was an expression used as a form of shorthand guidance to those who needed to be told that they had to coordinate their efforts with the MUP. Why would Pavkovic, do you think, refer to the Joint Command in a report to the Chief of the General Staff or chief of the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is my assessment that the duty team that drafted this report had in front of them the map or the order with the name of the Joint Command, and they are telling the superior command that the units would be engaged in that area in accordance with that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have 5D475.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you'll be familiar with this document. It's dated 12 March 2001, it's from you to the chief of the staff of the army, who at that time was General Pavkovic, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in this document you're asking him to request the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, who at that time was Mr. Kostunica, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were asking to be relieved of your duties as the then-commander of the 3rd Army, and it relates to the formation of a temporary Joint Command to control the joint forces of the VJ and police in a part of south Serbia at that time, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but let me be quite specific. This is not a Joint Command. The term used in Serbian is "zdruzena komanda." It is not the same term "zajednicka komanda," that we had been using so far, so this is a different term. It's a new term.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But an old concept?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to understand both terms because they're not defined anywhere. We're trying to understand them any which way we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, tell me, isn't your problem with this is that you see this body, whether we call it the Joint Command or the "zdruzena komand," your problem is you see it as interfering with the regular chain of command in the army, it creates a duality of command. That was your complaint and the reason that you were asking to be relieved of duty, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
